Both initial samples ( n =20) and convalescent samples ( n =40) were included. All confirmed and suspected COVID-19 patients had SARS-CoV-2-specific IgM, IgG and/or IgA antibodies detected by both IFA and neutralisation on one or more serum samples. Clinical data were available including date of symptom onset, SARSCoV-2 NAT results and possible exposure history. In SARS-CoV-2 seropositive samples, the presence of SARS-CoV-2-specific IgM and/or IgA were regarded as suggestive of a recent infection. Analytic sensitivity was low (27.3%–58.2%), analytic specificity was 88.3%–100%, clinical sensitivity was 45%–65%, and clinical specificity was 87.3%–100% [S1|PMC7508500_main|14240]. Sensitivity improved when specimens were collected more than 14 days after symptom onset [S2|PMC7508500_main|14240]. POCT-based antibody detection lagged behind immunofluorescence assay (IFA) by 0–9 days after disease onset [S3|PMC7508500_main|14240]. Due to poor sensitivity and delayed antibody detection, POCTs are considered unsuitable as a standalone diagnostic or screening tool for SARS-CoV-2 [S5|PMC7508500_main|14240].

map_chunks.summary_text: This chunk addresses the regulatory and performance landscape of point-of-care tests (POCTs) in the context of COVID-19 diagnosis in Australia. Twenty-two POCTs have been listed by the Australian TGA and are undergoing expedited post-marketing evaluation [S1|PMC7508500_main|14249]. Prior experience with antigen-detecting lateral flow assays (LFAs) for influenza demonstrated reduced sensitivity compared to nucleic acid testing (NAT) [S2|PMC7508500_main|14249]. Due to concerns over insufficient validation and potential misapplication of POCTs for COVID-19 diagnosis, multiple authoritative bodies — including the WHO, TGA, Public Health Laboratory Network, and The Royal College of Pathologists of Australasia — have issued cautions against their use in this context [S3|PMC7508500_main|14249].

findings.claim: Four POCTs evaluated: OnSite COVID-19 IgG/IgM Rapid Test (CTK Biotech), 2019-nCov Antibody Test (Innovita), SARS-CoV-2 Antibody Test Strip (Sinocare), Standard Q COVID-19 IgM/IgG Duo and Combo Tests (SD Biosensor)
findings.verbatim_support: We tested four different POCTs: OnSite COVID-19 IgG/IgM Rapid Test (CTK Biotech, USA), 2019-nCov Antibody Test (Innovita Tangshan Biological Technology, China), SARS-CoV-2 Antibody Test Strip (Changsha Sinocare, China), Standard Q COVID-19 IgM/IgG Duo Test and Standard Q COVID-19 IgM/IgG Combo Test (SD Biosensor, Republic of Korea). All are lateralflow assays that detect IgG and IgM antibodies against SARS-CoV-2 in whole blood, plasma or serum. The OnSite, Innovita and Standard Q Combo tests have separate lines containing anti-human IgG and IgM monoclonal antibodies, while the Sinocare test has a single line with both antibodies. The Standard Q Duo tests have separate individual devices for IgG and IgM, but are essentially the same test as the Standard Q Combo. There is a control line which must develop colour; if absent the test is invalid. They are promoted as tests to be used by healthcare professionals and the TGA restricts their use to medical practitioners.

findings.claim: COVID-19 cohort: 60 serum samples from 17 NAT-confirmed + 3 suspected (symptomatic household contacts) patients
findings.verbatim_support: Sixty serum samples were obtained from COVID-19 NAT-confirmed patients ( n =17) or COVID-19 suspected patients without positive NAT tests ( n =3) who were symptomatic household contacts of confirmed cases. The NAT method used was an in-house nucleic acid test targeting E gene and RdRp: the primers have been described elsewhere. Both initial samples ( n =20) and convalescent samples ( n =40) were included. All confirmed and suspected COVID-19 patients had SARS-CoV-2-specific IgM, IgG and/or IgA antibodies detected by both IFA and neutralisation on one or more serum samples. Clinical data were available including date of symptom onset, SARSCoV-2 NAT results and possible exposure history. In SARS-CoV-2 seropositive samples, the presence of SARS-CoV-2-specific IgM and/or IgA were regarded as suggestive of a recent infection. The detection of SARS-CoV-2specific IgG alone could not reliably be used to differentiate a past infection from a recent infection. SARS-CoV-2-specific IgG can often precede IgM or IgA following acute infection, and so the test should be interpreted within the context of the patient ' s date of symptom onset and potential exposure. This pattern has also been documented in SARS and SARS-CoV-2. -19

findings.claim: Analytic sensitivity defined as assay ability to detect SARS-CoV-2-specific antibodies when present in sera; clinical sensitivity defined as assay ability to identify patient's overall immune status to virus
findings.verbatim_support: Tang et al. highlighted the importance of distinguishing ' analytic ' and ' clinical ' sensitivity when assessing methods to detect COVID-19, namely the ability of an assay to detect SARS-CoV-2-specific antibodies when present in sera, versus the ability of an assay to identify a patient ' s overall immune status to the virus. The analytical sensitivity and specificity of each POCT was calculated independently for the presence of SARS-CoV-2-specific IgG and IgM in comparison to IFA. Clinical sensitivity was defined as the assessment of the overall development of antibodies in individual patients, and was measured as the detection of any antibody in any sample from a given patient. In addition, the clinical sensitivity and specificity of the test ' s ability to ascertain a correct immune status was assessed. Furthermore, we compared the sensitivity rate of specimens collected more than 14 days following onset of symptoms.

map_chunks.summary_text: This chunk describes the methodological framework used to evaluate SARS-CoV-2 point-of-care tests (POCTs). Following Tang et al.'s distinction [S1], the study separately quantifies (1) **analytical sensitivity/specificity** — the ability to detect SARS-CoV-2-specific IgG and IgM versus IFA as comparator [S2], and (2) **clinical sensitivity** — defined as detection of any antibody in any sample from a patient to reflect overall immune status [S3], with corresponding clinical specificity also assessed [S4]. Additionally, sensitivity rates were compared specifically for specimens collected more than 14 days after symptom onset [S5].

map_chunks.summary_text: This chunk (PMC7508500_main, C1) reports performance characteristics of four SARS-CoV-2 rapid lateral flow assays (Sinocare, Standard Q, OnSite, and Innovita) in a comparative serology evaluation. The Sinocare test showed cross-reactivity with samples positive for Mycoplasma pneumoniae IgM and influenza A serology [S1]. The Standard Q assay produced two false positives: one attributed to rheumatoid factor interference, and one in a SARS-CoV-2-uninfected patient [S2]. A subgroup of nine samples was identified as IgA-positive by IFA but IgM-negative by IFA, OnSite, and Innovita assays [S3]; the Standard Q IgM assay captured two of these nine [S4]. All nine had detectable SARS-CoV-2-specific IgG by IFA, yet sensitivity varied markedly among rapid assays: Innovita IgG detected none (0/9), OnSite IgG and Standard Q IgG each detected 3/9, and Sinocare detected only 1/9 [S5], highlighting substantial IgG detection gaps in rapid assays for IgA-dominant seroconverters.

map_chunks.summary_text: In this chunk [S1|PMC7508500_main|14266], two key observations are reported regarding antibody detection performance. First, there was a positive trend between increasing IgA, IgG, and IgM titres measured by IFA and improved detection rates. Second, in a serial serology sub-cohort of 3 patients, POCTs demonstrated a window period for antibody detection that was delayed by at least two days compared to IFA when measured from illness onset, indicating inferior early sensitivity of POCTs relative to IFA.

findings.verbatim_support: that this was not possible using POCTs. We recommend serial measurements using a quantitative assay (like IFA or neutralisation) to detect seroconversion or a rising titre as a more reliable method for timing infection than looking for the presence of SARS-CoV-2 specific IgM. Furthermore, we found SARS-CoV-2-specific IgA was frequently present in the absence of SARS-CoV-2-specific IgM by IFA, and in cases when they were both present, IgA was present in a higher titre, making it a more reliable serological marker of SARS-CoV-2 infection.
